1. **Chart type**: Scatter plot.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- Single-panel chart  
- No faceting or small multiples  
- No stacking  
- Repeated points for each year (many dots aligned vertically by year)

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Marathon time | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Pace per mile (shown as secondary scale text) | Quantitative | Secondary y-axis labels / annotation |
| Individual marathon performance (each of the 50 fastest per year) | Observational unit | Point mark |
| Point color | Categorical/nominal not visibly varying | Uniform pink color for all points (not used to encode a distinct variable) |

As a runner myself, I know that it’s pivotal that the more you run, the faster you get, which allows you to make great improvements over time. Beyond that, as communities of runners run more together, the true team comradery that comes from running really develops. Overall this graph is a testament to the women marathoners who have improved their running over time and as a result are running times faster than any of their kind have ever achieved.

comments.raw_comment:
"Runner's High-Female Marathoner Edition" 
As I look over the data that this graph is displaying, I notice that every couple years, the average marathon time for a woman improves about one to two minutes. This makes me wonder what causes this improvement...does their training change in terms of difficulty? Do they eat or drink something different during the race itself? We may never know the answer, unless we ask these female athletes. Growing up in a family of runners, including myself, I tend to follow in my family's footsteps when it comes to training, eating+sleeping habits, etc. Beyond that, my family has seen great success in this sport, which makes me curious to what point are these women changing their running-related rituals to gain such impressive times. Do they run 3 workouts a week, rather than 2 workouts a week? Do they snack before a run or workout? Again, going back to my previous comment, we will only know the answers if we ask the athlete experiencing the improvements.

comments.raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs:  "Was That the Flash or a Women Running the 26.2 Mile Dash?" by CB4 of California, "Going Going Gone: Womens Marathon Running is Picking up the Pace!” by Libby J of New Hampshire, and "Woman Marathon Runners Just Keep Getting Faster!" by Phoebe of Humboldt County, California.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back tomorrow --  Thursday afternoon, September 24 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs) or 
a slide show of 60 of our favorite graphs (tinyurl.com/NYT60Graphs).  
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who is a fast walker but not a marathoner,  and Chris Adkisson of Somerset, Kentucky, who lazily prefers a good Gilmore Girls marathon!

comments.raw_comment:
In the graph, the mean time for completion has increased by over 10 minutes. More notably, the gap of talent between the slowest and fastest runners has nearly halved from around 25 to 13 minutes. However, the peak times have not increased. The increase in average times is likely due to increased talent scouting and selection (pooling competitors from more countries, cities, etc) as well as a greater understanding of running biomechanics and training modalities. On the other hand, the top runner is roughly consistent with finishing times - meaning that shattering the previously conceived maximum human potential is very difficult. Genetically, these Women have not evolved - but the  level of competition in the event has. 
This is a shared phenomenon among many sports when the level of human potential is questioned. For example, the average baseball pitch is roughly 10 miles-per-hour faster than it was 20 years ago due to increased training and scouting, but the fastest pitch thrown in history has not changed since 1974.

1. The average running speed of the top 50 women marathoners has increased since 2000 (since the average time taken to run the marathon has decreased). This seems to particularly be due to an increase towards the bottom of the spread on the graph.

Now, with a growing population, that seems obvious, but I wonder if the rate of change in the running speed might be affected by certain factors relating to women's sports in particular. For example, if most women who would be achieving top marathon times would be in their 20s, did the average speed of women running marathons increase faster than usual during the 90s, when the first generations affected by Title IX and the increasing gender parity in school sports reached that age? How does this correlate with standards of living in general? And what do the averages look like for all women finishing marathons?
3. It is certainly heartening to see that athletes are getting fitter over time, though I can't say what this means for gender equality without comparing it to the times for men. Broadly speaking, it's a positive trend.
4. "Top Women Runners Getting Faster" (I tried to be catchy without getting less accurate, but it is a bit vague; I don't know how to make the word "marathon" catchy).

comments.raw_comment:
Women, without doubt, have become more agile when running marathons in the past 20 years. At the start of the century, their range was between 2:47:00 and 2:27:00. Now, their times have dropped to around 2:35:00 through 2:22:00. That means that their maximum time has decreased by nearly 12 minutes and their minimum by 5 minutes. Furthermore, the female's times have become more spread out. Meaning, the dots on the graph have become more dispersed, instead of being concentrated at the maximum times. One other trend I observed is that there were fewer runners recorded in the past couple years. I did some tedious counting and found out that around the start of the graph, there were about 70 athletes, but in the more recent years, about 40 athletes have competed. In summary, women have improved their times for running marathons, however they also have grown to be fewer and farther between. 

I wonder if this tendency also applies to men?

This perseverance and dedication proves to me that it is possible to improve anything, even when I may think it is already flawless.

My graph's headline would be: "Catch Me if You Ever Can".

comments.raw_comment:
1. There's an upward trend in women's top marathon times over the past two decades. The average top time each year seems to be getting smaller (meaning the runners are getting faster). 

2. I wonder why the outlier times (the very fastest 2-3 times each year) don't follow a similar trend as the average. And what could be causing the increase in the general population, that isn't reflected in the very top runners? 

I'm also curious about which dots represent the same women, and what other information could be gleaned if you looked at the trajectories of individual women over time. I'm interested in whether each dot represents a distinct woman or a distinct time (i.e. could the same woman be responsible for multiple dots in the same year?)

I also wonder what this same graph would look like with the 50 fastest men's marathons. 

3. This suggests something to me about women's achievement in athletics (we keep getting better and better over time!) and makes me excited about the future of women athletes. Growth is achievable, and the graph encourages me to have patience with myself and my communities, because these marathoners' growth occurred over decades.
